hints: Look at both properties together, because first ionisation energy generally rises across Period 3 but with two famous dips, while melting point rises to silicon then falls sharply.
Focus on phosphorus, which is higher in first ionisation energy than both its neighbours due to its stable half-filled 3p subshell, and has a very low melting point as a simple molecular solid.
Test each consecutive trio by asking which middle element can beat both neighbours for ionisation energy and also be the lowest melting, then match it to the table.
walkthrough:
**Recall the Period 3 first ionisation energy trend**

Remember that first ionisation energy generally increases left to right due to increasing nuclear charge. But there are two dips: $\text{Mg} > \text{Al}$ and $\text{P} > \text{S}$.

This is due to subshell stability: $\text{Mg}$ ($\text{3s}^2$) is more stable than $\text{Al}$ ($\text{3s}^2\text{3p}^1$), and $\text{P}$ ($\text{3s}^2\text{3p}^3$ half-filled) is more stable than $\text{S}$ ($\text{3s}^2\text{3p}^4$).

**Recall the Period 3 melting point trend**

Melting point rises from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Si}$ as metallic bonding gets stronger then giant covalent bonding appears. Then it drops sharply at $\text{P}$.

$\text{Si}$ (giant covalent, mp ~1414 C) is very high, while $\text{P}$ ($\text{P}_4$ molecules, mp ~44 C) and $\text{S}$ ($\text{S}_8$ molecules, mp ~115 C) are low with weak van der Waals forces between molecules.

**Apply both clues to element Y**

Y must have the highest first ionisation energy of its trio. That points to either $\text{Mg}$ (beating $\text{Na}$ and $\text{Al}$) or $\text{P}$ (beating $\text{Si}$ and $\text{S}$).

Y must also have the lowest melting point of its trio. $\text{Mg}$ is not the lowest in $\text{Na}$, $\text{Mg}$, $\text{Al}$ because $\text{Na}$ melts much lower. $\text{P}$ is the lowest in $\text{Si}$, $\text{P}$, $\text{S}$ because $\text{Si}$ is giant and $\text{S}_8$ has stronger van der Waals than $\text{P}_4$.

**Identify X, Y and Z**

So Y must be phosphorus. Since X, Y and Z are consecutive, X is the element before and Z is the element after.

That gives $\text{X} = \text{Si}$, $\text{Y} = \text{P}$, $\text{Z} = \text{S}$.

options.A: Mg does have the highest first ionisation energy of Na, Mg, Al (738 > 496 and 578 kJ mol-1), but it does not have the lowest melting point. Na melts at ~98 C, much lower than Mg at ~650 C, so Y fails the second condition.
options.B: In Mg, Al, Si the highest first ionisation energy is Si (~786 kJ mol-1), not Al (~578 kJ mol-1). Al is actually the lowest of the three due to the Mg to Al dip, so Y fails the ionisation energy condition.
options.C: In Al, Si, P the highest first ionisation energy is P (~1012 kJ mol-1), not Si (~786 kJ mol-1). Also the lowest melting point is P (~44 C), not Si (~1414 C). So Si as Y fails both conditions.
options.D: In Si, P, S, phosphorus has the highest first ionisation energy (~1012 kJ mol-1) beating Si (~786) and S (~1000) because of its stable half-filled 3p3 configuration. It also has the lowest melting point (~44 C) compared to giant covalent Si (~1414 C) and S8 (~115 C). Both conditions fit perfectly.
